claims.text: The initial particles are sub-10 nm, approximately 5–8 nm, equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by rapid quenching or inert-gas condensation.
Above 600 K, sluggish diffusion is overwhelmed by surface-energy-driven Ostwald ripening and spinodal decomposition.
Heating above 600 K causes rapid phase separation rather than preservation of entropy-stabilized homogeneity.
A high surface-to-volume ratio creates a high surface-energy gradient in the nanoparticles.
The surface-energy gradient lowers the activation barrier for surface diffusion and atomic exchange.
Enhanced surface diffusion bypasses the constraint of sluggish bulk diffusion.
The smallest particles drive a surface-diffusion-limited Ostwald-ripening process.
Au and Cu segregate to particle surfaces or form distinct domains.
Pt, Co, and Ni coalesce into larger cores.
The proposed surface-mediated kinetic pathway proceeds faster than configurational-entropy-driven mixing.
The pathway produces a core-shell or multiphase structure instead of a homogeneous solid solution.
Particles smaller than 5 nm are disproportionately lost through dissolution or evaporation of surface atoms.
Larger particles grow after loss of the smallest particles.
The larger particles develop a Pt/Ni-rich core and an Au/Cu-rich shell.
Particles larger than 20 nm may retain homogeneity longer because bulk sluggish diffusion may dominate.
Heating more slowly than 1 K/min may permit equilibrium thermodynamic stabilization and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Reactive atmospheric species can change surface energies and invalidate the proposed regime.
The hypothesis is falsified if sub-10 nm particles remain single-phase without a significant size-distribution shift through 900 K under the specified comparison with larger particles.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as single-phase, yet phase separation into Au-rich and Pt-rich domains is said to cause a reduction in the number of distinct phases. Relative to a single-phase initial state, formation of compositionally distinct domains would ordinarily increase, not reduce, the number of phases.

The headline hypothesis invokes both spinodal decomposition and Ostwald ripening, but the detailed mechanism only develops a surface-diffusion-limited Ostwald-ripening pathway and does not explain the compositional instability required for spinodal decomposition.
